name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,826

entries.clue: Decadent holiday starts with Jeff losing case (6)

indicatorNotes.starts with: Whatever a word starts with takes its opening squares, so the piece named after this phrase goes in front of the one named before it.
indicatorNotes.losing case: A case is the shell a thing travels in, and a word losing its case gives up the letters at either end.

blocks.note: JEFF stripped of the J and the F that case it keeps only its middle pair
a fete is a village holiday with stalls and a bottle tombola

annotation.surface: A decadent holiday that begins with Jeff mislaying his suitcase.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Case' is luggage in the surface and a word's outer shell in the wordplay, so Jeff hands over his middle. Fete for a holiday is the French feast day naturalised.
annotation.definitionFit: Effete means drained and over-refined, the sense 'decadent' carries when it describes a civilisation past its best.

entries.clue: Grip plum, having bitten a third off (6)

indicatorNotes.having bitten: A bite takes a piece clean out of whatever it lands on, so the letters it names are gone before anything else happens.
indicatorNotes.off: A third off a price is a third taken away, and the same fraction comes away from the word here.

blocks.note: a greengage is a small green plum, nine letters to start from
a third of nine letters is three, and these are the three at the front

annotation.surface: A plum held in the hand with a third of it already bitten away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grip' is the definition and a verb, so the answer has to be a verb too. 'A third' counts letters rather than mouthfuls, which is what makes the plum worth naming in full.
annotation.definitionFit: To engage a gear or an enemy is to take hold of it and not let go, which is what 'grip' asks for in the same transitive way.

entries.clue: Bob Marley among others in castle, initially (3,1,5)

indicatorNotes.in: Something in a castle is within its walls, so the letters named before this word are planted inside the word named after it.

blocks.note: a fort is a castle, and it opens up after its first two letters
Marley was the most famous Rasta of all, one among many

annotation.surface: Bob Marley and other acts billed to play a castle.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma after 'castle' makes 'initially' look like part of the billing, and it is the definition. Rasta is short for Rastafarian, the Jamaican faith Marley belonged to.
annotation.definitionFit: 'For a start' is what you say before the first item of a list, which is the job 'initially' does in a sentence.

entries.clue: Murphy's one to argue against getting up (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition runs backwards: a murphy is Irish slang for a potato, and the answer names the class of thing one of those is.

indicatorNotes.getting up: Getting up is travel towards the top of the page, so in a down entry these letters are read from the bottom square upwards.

blocks.note: to rebut a claim is to argue against it, and those five letters are set down from the foot of the column up

annotation.surface: Murphy is the sort who will argue against ever getting out of bed.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface has Murphy objecting to an early start; the wordplay reads 'getting up' as a direction of travel instead. Murphy is an Irish nickname for the potato.
annotation.definitionFit: A murphy is a potato and a potato is a tuber, the swollen underground stem a plant stores its food in.

entries.clue: A newspaper's covering gendarme's troubles (8)

indicatorNotes.covering: A cover goes over what it hides, so the letters named before it wrap round the ones named after.

blocks.note: the clue's own first word, taken at face value
the Financial Times is the FT, and the possessive adds the S
flic is French slang for a policeman, what a gendarme is called on the street

annotation.surface: A newspaper reporting on the difficulties of a French policeman.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Covering' is a journalist's word in the surface and a wrapper in the wordplay. FT for the Financial Times is standard, and the apostrophe-s is quietly part of the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To afflict someone is to trouble them with pain or hardship, so 'troubles' is the same verb in the same person.

entries.clue: Helpful woman just not the same after my dog exploded (5,9)

indicatorNotes.exploded: An explosion scatters whatever it hits, so those letters land in a new order.
indicatorNotes.after: What comes after something follows it down the column, so this piece takes the squares below the ones just named.

blocks.note: a just settlement is a fair one
five letters of fodder
another one is not the same one

annotation.surface: A helpful woman has not been herself since my dog blew up.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a sad anecdote, with 'just' meaning simply; in the wordplay it means fair. 'After' is not scene-setting either — it says which piece follows which.
annotation.definitionFit: A fairy godmother is the figure who turns up to fix everything, and the phrase is now used of any woman who unexpectedly helps.

entries.clue: Attend new Hamlet, say, halfway through Lear (4,2,3)

indicatorNotes.halfway through: Halfway through a word is its midpoint, so the letters named go in where the four-letter name splits in two.

blocks.note: the play's title, opened down the middle
n is the standard abbreviation for new
Hamlet is the Prince of Denmark, so he is one example of a Dane

annotation.surface: A theatregoer taking in a new Hamlet halfway through a run of Lear.
annotation.walkthrough: Two Shakespeare tragedies, and only one of them is being staged here: Lear is four letters to be prised apart, Hamlet a nationality. 'Attend' is the old sense, to listen.
annotation.definitionFit: To attend in its older sense is to listen — attend to me — and lending an ear is giving someone exactly that hearing.

entries.clue: Shin up branch following child's lead (5)

indicatorNotes.following: What follows something comes along behind it, so the piece named first takes the lower squares of the column.
indicatorNotes.lead: A lead is what goes out in front, so a word's lead is the single letter it begins with.

blocks.note: the first letter of CHILD
a branch of a tree is a limb

annotation.surface: Going up a branch by following where a child went first.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Following' does positional work: in a down entry the branch sits below what it follows. 'Shin up' is the whole definition — shinning is hauling yourself up with arms and legs round a trunk.
annotation.definitionFit: To shin up a drainpipe or a tree is to climb it, so the phrasal verb and the plain one swap straight over.

entries.clue: Notice son in terror kept rising and sinking (8)

blocks.note: to notice something is to see it
s is the standard abbreviation for son
somebody in terror is awed, struck silent by what faces them

annotation.surface: A son's terror going up and down while you watch it.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is a verb built from three words that none of them look like verbs. Terror here is the awe-struck kind rather than the screaming kind, which is what lets an adjective in.
annotation.definitionFit: A seesaw's two ends go up and down by turns, so a thing that seesawed kept rising and sinking in just that alternating way.

entries.clue: Find your bottle - chance new dog has swallowed beer? (5,2,7)

indicatorNotes.has swallowed: What has been swallowed ends up inside the swallower, so these letters go within the ones named just before.

blocks.note: a new dog is a pup, three letters to open up
a chance of winning is a piece of luck
Courage is a British brewery whose bitter is sold in pubs nationwide, so it is one beer among many

annotation.surface: Wondering whether the new dog has drunk your beer, and being told to find your bottle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' is nerve in British slang rather than glassware, which is the joke sitting next to the beer. The question mark flags a brewer's name standing in for beer itself.
annotation.definitionFit: Bottle is British slang for nerve, so finding yours means gathering the courage to go through with something frightening.

entries.clue: Cheap supermarket by habit stocking one sort of biscuit (9)

indicatorNotes.stocking: A shop stocking an item keeps it inside, so the letter named next goes within the word just given.

blocks.note: a monk's habit is his garb
the Roman numeral for one
Aldi is the German-owned discount chain on British high streets

annotation.surface: A discount supermarket that always has one kind of biscuit on the shelves.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stocking' is shop language in the surface and an insertion instruction underneath. The biscuit is the flat currant one British children call a squashed-fly biscuit, named after the Italian general.
annotation.definitionFit: A Garibaldi is a currant-filled biscuit sold in British packets, so 'sort of biscuit' names it by the class it belongs to.

entries.clue: Simple coming back through Cambridge via Newmarket (5)

indicatorNotes.coming back: Coming back is the return leg, so the run of letters is read from its far end to its near one.
indicatorNotes.through: A road through two towns passes inside them, and the letters wanted run inside the words the same way.

blocks.note: the run E-VIA-N straddles those three words, and it is taken the other way round

annotation.surface: Driving back through Cambridge by way of Newmarket.
annotation.walkthrough: Two town names and the word between them hide the letters — Newmarket is the racing town just east of Cambridge. 'Simple' here means trusting rather than easy.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone naive is simple in the old sense of unworldly and easily taken in, the way a country cousin is called simple.

entries.clue: Talk German equally (3)

blocks.note: g is the standard abbreviation for German
as tall as the next man uses as for equally

annotation.surface: Speaking German just as well as the next person.
annotation.walkthrough: Three words, three jobs and no indicator at all, so the solver has to spot that 'equally' is a word to be translated rather than an instruction. Gas for idle talk is Victorian slang that stuck.
annotation.definitionFit: To gas is to talk on and on about nothing much, so 'talk' is the same verb with a windbag attached.

entries.clue: Adrian's muscly boyfriend Clark tangled with a yobbo (5,6)

indicatorNotes.tangled with: Two things tangled with each other end up in a heap, no longer in the order they arrived in.

blocks.note: five letters of fodder
six more, eleven in all — a yobbo is British slang for a loutish young thug

annotation.surface: Adrian's muscly boyfriend Clark has got into a brawl with a lout.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder hides in plain sight: 'Clark' reads as the boyfriend's name and is really five letters for scrambling. Adrian is the shy shop girl of the Rocky films.
annotation.definitionFit: In the Rocky films Adrian is courted and married by the hulking Philadelphia boxer, so he is her muscly boyfriend before he is her husband.

entries.clue: Win gold for old coach (6)

blocks.note: to land a contract is to win it
au is the chemical symbol for gold

annotation.surface: Winning a gold medal for an old coach.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Coach' is the trap — the surface makes it the trainer at the trackside, and it is a carriage. Landing a deal and winning one are the same verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A landau is the four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage with a folding hood still brought out for royal processions.

entries.clue: Flag seen in Copenhagen and Borgen all over the place (9)

indicatorNotes.all over the place: Things all over the place are in no order at all, so the letters just named are to be rearranged.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder — Borgen is the Danish political drama, which is why it is in italics

annotation.surface: A flag turning up in Copenhagen and in Borgen too.
annotation.walkthrough: 'And' is fodder rather than joinery, which is the hardest kind of anagram to see. The italics are doing real work: they mark a programme title, not a place.
annotation.definitionFit: The Dannebrog is Denmark's white-crossed red flag, flown all over Copenhagen and claimed as the oldest national flag still in use.

entries.clue: Concerning condensation reported late (7)

indicatorNotes.reported: A word reported is passed on by mouth, so what counts is how it sounds rather than how it is spelt.

blocks.note: a row over money is a row concerning money
the condensation that settles on grass overnight is dew, and this is the other spelling of that sound

annotation.surface: A late report about condensation.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Concerning' is the preposition here, not the adjective meaning worrying. 'Reported' is the sound signal, and what it points at is the moisture of a cold morning.
annotation.definitionFit: A library book kept past its date or a bill left unpaid is overdue, which is simply late in the strict sense.

entries.clue: Work schedule marked up, one sets off (9)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a relative clause with its 'that' dropped — the one that sets off a charge — which is how the setter gets a noun out of a verb phrase.

indicatorNotes.up: In a down entry up means from the bottom square towards the top, so the letters named are read backwards.

blocks.note: a rota is the list saying who works which shift, and it goes in from the foot of the column up
a marked improvement is a noted one, and it is reversed along with the rest

annotation.surface: The shift rota is marked up on the wall and one worker sets off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sets off' is the pivot: departure in the surface, ignition in the answer. Both pieces of wordplay are reversed in a single move, so 'up' turns nine letters at once.
annotation.definitionFit: A detonator is the small charge that sets off the main explosive, so 'one sets off' names it by the single job it exists to do.

entries.clue: Break from work initially suits head servant (8)

indicatorNotes.initially: Initially means at the very start, so only the first letter of the word beside it is wanted.

blocks.note: the first letter of SUITS
the head of a list is its top
a page is the boy servant who runs errands in a great house

annotation.surface: A walkout that suits the head servant well enough at first.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Suits' looks like the verb holding the sentence together and is only there for its first letter. Head and top are the same word in a hundred clues, which is worth banking.
annotation.definitionFit: A stoppage is the industrial word for work halted, whether by strike or breakdown, which is exactly a break from work.

entries.clue: Massive cuckoo feeds little bird, start of contrition? (7)

indicatorNotes.feeds: Feeding something in pushes it inside, so the piece named before this word slots into the letters named after it.
indicatorNotes.start of: The start of a word is the letter it begins with, and that single letter is all that is taken.

blocks.note: a tit is the small garden bird of the blue tit and the great tit
the ani is a black tropical cuckoo and a regular in crosswords
the first letter of CONTRITION

annotation.surface: A guilty cuckoo feeding the little bird whose nest it invaded.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a cuckoo making amends, which is funny because cuckoos do the reverse — the host bird feeds the interloper's chick. Massive comes from the Titans of Greek myth.
annotation.definitionFit: Titanic means on the scale of the Titans, the giant elder gods of Greek myth, which is to say massive.

entries.clue: Mike tries developing good qualities (6)

indicatorNotes.developing: Something developing is changing shape as it grows, so the letters beside it settle into a different arrangement.

blocks.note: Mike is M in the radio alphabet
five letters of fodder

annotation.surface: Mike having a go at developing some good qualities.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mike' is the radio alphabet rather than a man, which the capital letter is allowed to hide. Once he has handed over his single letter the anagram is only five letters long.
annotation.definitionFit: The merits of a case are the points in its favour, so a list of merits is a list of good qualities.

entries.clue: Lifted German's fruit loaf that's one pound lighter (6)

indicatorNotes.lighter: Something a pound lighter has had that pound taken off it, so the letter standing for the pound goes.

blocks.note: stollen is the German Christmas loaf full of dried fruit and marzipan
l is the standard abbreviation for pound, and only one of the two here comes out

annotation.surface: A German fruit loaf that weighs a pound less than it did.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' is the shoplifter's word, which is the definition hiding in a baking scene. 'One pound lighter' sounds like weight and means one letter.
annotation.definitionFit: To lift something is to steal it — shoplifters lift goods — so 'lifted' is the past participle the answer matches exactly.

entries.clue: Show freezer a year on, full of good rump (5,6)

indicatorNotes.full of: A thing full of something has it inside, so the letters named after the phrase sit within the ones named before.

blocks.note: pa is per annum, the Latin for a year that turns up on salaries
what is the good of it and what is the use of it ask the same question
a butt is a backside, the rump of an animal
the clue's own word, taken at face value

annotation.surface: A freezer opened a year on, still full of good rump steak.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Show freezer' is the definition and reads as kitchen equipment. In the wordplay 'good' is the noun of 'what's the good of it', which is the step that hides longest.
annotation.definitionFit: Pressing pause freezes the picture where it stands, so the button that does it is literally the thing that freezes a show.

entries.clue: Absolute crackpot whose head has gone (5)

indicatorNotes.has gone: What has gone is no longer there, so the letter named just before it is dropped.

blocks.note: a nutter is British slang for a crackpot
the head of the word is the letter at the front of it

annotation.surface: An absolute crackpot who has lost his head.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Absolute' and 'crackpot' both want to be the definition, and the adjective is the one that leaves a word for the wordplay to behead. Losing your head is the joke twice over.
annotation.definitionFit: Utter nonsense is absolute nonsense: the adjective only works in front of a noun, which is how 'absolute' is used here too.

entries.clue: Picture from life-drawing class includes good elbow (5)

indicatorNotes.includes: Whatever a thing includes is found inside it, so the letter named next goes within the word just given.

blocks.note: the picture made in a life-drawing class is a nude, worked from an unclothed model
g is the standard abbreviation for good

annotation.surface: A life class picture with a well-drawn elbow in it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Elbow' is the definition and it is a verb — you elbow someone in a crowd. The surface keeps it a body part in a drawing, which is the whole misdirection.
annotation.definitionFit: To elbow someone in a queue is to give them a small dig with the arm, which is what it is to nudge them.

entries.clue: Our usual base turned clear (3)

indicatorNotes.turned: Turned round means facing the other way, so the letters are read from the end back to the start.

blocks.note: we all count in base ten, and those three letters are set down backwards

annotation.walkthrough: 'Base' is the number base we count in rather than a camp or a chemical. 'Clear' is the money sense: to net a sum is to clear it once everything has been deducted.
annotation.definitionFit: A trader who nets a hundred pounds clears that much after costs, so the two verbs describe the same leftover sum.

entries.clue: Table set with candles, bread and wine, cook heard? (5)

annotation.definition: Table set with candles, bread and wine

indicatorNotes.heard: Heard means taken by ear, so the word wanted is the one that sounds like the clue's word rather than the one spelt that way.

blocks.note: to cook the books is to alter them, and the two words are said exactly alike

annotation.surface: A table laid with candles, bread and wine, and a cook overheard nearby.
annotation.walkthrough: Cooking the books is doctoring them, which is the sense the clue wants from a kitchen word. The table described is the communion table at the east end of a church.
annotation.definitionFit: An altar is the church table where the bread and wine of communion are consecrated, candles standing either side of it.

entries.clue: Criminal acted alone mostly, according to reports (9)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a phrase doing an adjective's work: evidence held 'according to reports' is precisely the kind the answer describes.

indicatorNotes.Criminal: A criminal act is a crooked one, and crooked letters are letters knocked out of their proper order.
indicatorNotes.mostly: Mostly means most but not all, so the word beside it gives up its last letter.

blocks.note: five letters of fodder
most of ALONE is the first four of its five letters

annotation.surface: A criminal who acted alone, at least according to the reports.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' opens the clue as the man everything else describes, and it is the anagram signal. The definition is the tail: hearsay evidence rather than proof.
annotation.definitionFit: Anecdotal evidence is what people report having seen rather than what has been measured, so it stands only according to reports.

entries.clue: Half fat separates before long in tea (4,4)

indicatorNotes.separates: What separates something comes between its parts, so these letters split the word named beside them in two.

blocks.note: something happening before long happens early
fat is grease, and half of its six letters is the first three

annotation.surface: Half the fat separating out in the tea before long.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Separates' is an insertion instruction, not a description of what fat does in a cup. The tea is black leaf scented with bergamot, named after an 1830s prime minister.
annotation.definitionFit: Earl Grey is one of the standard British blends, so 'tea' defines it by the class of drink it belongs to.

entries.clue: Starmer entered for bike race (6)

blocks.note: Sir Keir Starmer leads the British Labour party, and it is his first name that is wanted
a rider entered for a race is in it

annotation.surface: Starmer signing up for a cycle race.
annotation.walkthrough: A surname in a clue usually hands over the surname; this one asks for the forename instead. The race is the Olympic track event in which riders follow a pacing motorbike.
annotation.definitionFit: A keirin is a track cycling race where riders sit behind a motorised pacer until it pulls off and they sprint for the line.
